title: About taxodist
text:
taxodist is an open-source project for retrieving ordered taxonomic lineages and measuring separation between nodes in a classification hierarchy. It is available as coordinated R, Python, and Julia packages and through an interactive web application.
The project addresses a practical need: a reproducible way to resolve taxon names, inspect their lineages, identify their most recent common ancestor, and construct labeled distance objects for downstream analysis.
The current implementation uses lineage data from The Taxonomicon, based on Systema Naturae 2000. The external source remains responsible for the underlying classification; taxodist retrieves, cleans, organizes, and compares those records.

title: About taxodist
text:
Methodological position
By default, the distance between distinct hierarchy nodes is the reciprocal of MRCA depth. Identical complete lineages receive distance zero. Within a connected hierarchy, this produces an ultrametric. Path-length, Wu–Palmer, and rank-based distances are available as explicit alternatives.
These values measure classification depth. They do not estimate evolutionary time, genetic or morphological divergence, phylogenetic branch length, or statistical support for ancestry. The interpretation of every analysis is conditional on the source classification and the intermediate nodes it records.
Version 0.6.0 formalized this distinction across the R package, Python package, application, reference data, and documentation. Version 0.7.0 optimized cached matrix construction. Version 0.8.0 added auditable resolution records, offline user-supplied classifications, and portable analysis bundles shared by all three implementations. Version 0.9.0 corrected retrieval and caching errors and added classification trees, distances between two sets of taxa, and the comparison of repeated analyses. Version 1.0.0, the first stable release, replaced the text-based lineage parser with one that reads the structure of each Taxonomicon page, retained the rank of every node, added alternative distance metrics and the taxonomic distinctness indices of Clarke and Warwick, and froze the metric definitions and the bundle format for the 1.x series.

title: About taxodist
text:
Project history
The project began with a general question: how can the shared hierarchical position of any two named organisms be retrieved and compared programmatically?
Early development focused on resolving names and parsing the deeply nested classification exposed by The Taxonomicon. Subsequent releases added matrix operations, lineage comparison, cache persistence, visualization, multivariate helpers, offline reference data, Python and Julia implementations with matching distance semantics, and diversity indices.
The project remains deliberately focused on classification-based analysis. It does not attempt to replace curated phylogenies, sequence-based inference, divergence-time estimation, or specialized taxonomic name services.

R stores only the lower triangle in a compact dist object. Convert it when a square matrix is required:
d <- distance_matrix(taxa)
m <- as.matrix(d)

title: Cross-language Compatibility
text:
Clustering and ordination
The analysis results are semantically aligned but use different numerical ecosystems.

Clustering
R delegates to stats::hclust(), Python to SciPy, and Julia to Clustering.jl. With the same complete finite matrix and equivalent method, all three summarize the same dissimilarities, although internal merge representations and plotting defaults differ.


Ordination
All three implementations perform classical multidimensional scaling and return:

points;
the underlying dist or distance DataFrame;
GOF goodness-of-fit values;
eig eigenvalues.

Coordinate signs may differ between numerical implementations because eigenvectors are defined only up to sign. A sign reversal of an axis does not change the represented geometry or pairwise distances.






Compare geometry, not axis orientation



When validating ordinations across languages, compare eigenvalues and Euclidean distances among coordinates. Do not require every coordinate column to have the same sign.

title: Cross-language Compatibility
text:
Plotting and console output
R uses S3 methods such as print(), plot(), and summary(). Python and Julia expose explicit helpers such as plot_taxodist_cluster(), plot_taxodist_ord(), and summary_taxodist_ord(). Plotting is optional in both: Python needs pip install "taxodist[plot]", and Julia loads its plotting code only after using Plots.
Typography, plotting backends, colors, dendrogram orientation, and console formatting are not part of the cross-language compatibility contract. Scientific values, labels, and structural fields are.

title: Cross-language Compatibility
text:
Version 1.0.0 validation

Parser. The three implementations share trimmed copies of real Taxonomicon pages and a file of expected lineages, and each test suite checks its structured parser against them. The text fallback parser of Julia is also checked against output generated with R.
Metrics and bundles. Distances under the four metrics, and bundles of schema 1.1, are checked against the R implementation; bundles written by Python are read by R and vice versa for every metric.
Distinctness. taxo_distinctness() reproduces vegan::taxondive() in R, and the Python and Julia implementations return the same values as R.
Reference data. taxobase was rebuilt in R with the new parser and exported to the neutral JSON file loaded by Python and Julia.
Coverage. Each implementation reports complete line coverage under its language-specific coverage measure.

Version 0.9.0 validation and performance

Bundle interoperability
Release 0.9.0 was checked with a common set of user-supplied lineages that included an ancestor–descendant pair, two inputs with identical lineages, and a lineage with a different root (infinite distances). Each implementation built a bundle with taxo_from_lineages() and taxo_bundle(), wrote it to JSON, and read the bundles written by the other two. In all six reader–writer combinations, compare_bundles() reported no changed taxa and no changed distances, and every matrix agreed with the R matrix to within \(10^{-12}\).

Matrices are now computed from integer identifiers of each node’s complete path from the root. title: Cross-language Compatibility
text:
Cache compatibility
Cache contents have the same conceptual keys—resolved IDs and lineages—but the files are intentionally not interchangeable:

R uses saveRDS() and .rds files;
Python uses pickle and .pkl files;
Julia uses JSON and .json files.

Do not rename one format to imitate another. For a cross-language archival record, use the portable bundle format introduced in version 0.8.0.
In all three implementations, cleaned and uncleaned lineages are cached under separate keys (lin_<id> and rawlin_<id>), as are their ranks (ranks_<id> and rawranks_<id>), and save_cache() and load_cache() default to a persistent per-user location when no file is given. Cache files record the parser version (meta_parser_version); lineages from files written before version 1.0.0 are discarded on loading, and their taxon identifiers are kept.






Untrusted Python cache files



Only load .pkl files from trusted sources. Python’s pickle format can execute code during deserialization.

title: Introduction to taxodist
Introduction to taxodist
Introduction to taxodist
text:
The distance definition
For two ordered lineages \(L_A\) and \(L_B\), the MRCA is the final node in their continuous common prefix. The metric is
\[
d(A,B)=
\begin{cases}
0, & L_A = L_B, \\
\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA})}, & L_A \neq L_B.
\end{cases}
\]
The root has depth 1. Consequently, distinct nodes sharing only that root have distance 1, while a deeper MRCA produces a smaller positive value.
Zero is reserved for identical hierarchy nodes. If one queried node is an ancestor of the other, their distance remains positive. Use is_member() when your question is about containment and taxo_path() when you want to inspect the route between nodes.
This reciprocal distance is the default. Other metrics are described in Alternative distance metrics below.
Within a connected hierarchy, this definition is an ultrametric. Valid Taxonomicon lineages share the retained root Biota; infinite distance is a defensive result for disconnected input lineages. If a lineage cannot be retrieved, the corresponding values are missing (NA in R and NaN in Python or Julia matrices).






Interpretation



Classification depth depends on the source and on which intermediate clades it records. These distances must not be interpreted as genetic divergence, morphological difference, evolutionary time, or phylogenetic branch length.

Alternative distance metrics
The metric argument of taxo_distance(), distance_matrix(), cross_distances(), focal_distances(), closest_relative(), taxo_heatmap(), and taxo_bundle() selects the distance. With \(h\) the MRCA depth and \(d_A\), \(d_B\) the lineage depths:

Distance
Use




"reciprocal" (default)
\(1/h\)
Ultrametric; emphasizes shallow divergences


"path"
\(d_A + d_B - 2h\)
Number of edges between the two nodes


"wu_palmer"
\(1 - 2h/(d_A + d_B)\)
Normalizes for the uneven resolution of different groups


"ranked"
Half the path through the standard Linnaean ranks
Step weights of Clarke and Warwick: 1 for congeneric, 2 for confamilial species, …

Clustering, ordination, and heatmaps
The analysis helpers accept taxon names or a previously computed distance object.

RPythonJulia


distances <- distance_matrix(taxa)

cluster <- taxo_cluster(distances)
ordination <- taxo_ordinate(distances, k = 2)

plot(cluster)

plot(ordination)

plot_taxodist_ord(ordination)

Check the matrix first



Clustering, ordination, and heatmaps require at least two taxa and a finite, complete distance matrix. The helpers warn and return an empty analysis component when the matrix contains missing or infinite distances.


When names are supplied instead of a matrix, metric and the other arguments of distance_matrix() can be passed to taxo_cluster(), taxo_ordinate(), and taxo_heatmap(). In Python, the plotting functions require pip install "taxodist[plot]".
The clustering dendrogram is a visualization of taxonomic hierarchy distances. It is not a phylogeny inferred from characters, sequences, or branch lengths.

title: Introduction to taxodist
text:
Classification trees
taxo_tree() represents the classification itself as a tree, without a clustering step. Internal nodes are the named clades at which the supplied taxa diverge, and clades with a single descendant are collapsed. Branch lengths are chosen so that patristic distances in the tree equal the values returned by distance_matrix().

RPythonJulia


tree <- taxo_tree(taxa)          # an ape-compatible "phylo" object
tree$node.label

library(ape)
plot(tree, show.node.label = TRUE)
write.tree(tree)                 # Newick


tree = td.taxo_tree(taxa)        # a TaxodistTree
tree.node_label
tree.to_newick()                 # for Bio.Phylo, ete3, DendroPy, ...
tree.cophenetic()                # equals td.distance_matrix(taxa)


tree = taxo_tree(taxa)           # a TaxodistTree
tree.node_label
newick(tree)
cophenetic(tree)                 # equals distance_matrix(taxa)



Unlike a clustering dendrogram, the tree keeps polytomies where the classification records several clades at the same node, and labels every split with its clade name. It remains a representation of the classification, not an inferred phylogeny. All lineages must share the same root; taxa without a lineage are dropped with a warning. The branch lengths reproduce the default reciprocal distance.

title: Introduction to taxodist
text:
Taxonomic diversity and distinctness
taxo_distinctness() computes the indices of Warwick and Clarke for one or more samples: taxonomic diversity (Δ), taxonomic distinctness (Δ*), average taxonomic distinctness (Δ+), and variation in taxonomic distinctness (Λ+). Samples are given as a vector of names (presence only) or as a table with one row per sample and one column per taxon. By default distances use the "ranked" metric, which reproduces the classical step weights; any other metric, or a precomputed matrix, can be supplied.
The example below uses curated lineages with ranks, so it runs offline.

RPythonJulia


standard <- c(NA, "Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus")
lineages <- list(
  Panthera = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Mammalia", "Carnivora", "Felidae", "Panthera"),
  Felis    = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Mammalia", "Carnivora", "Felidae", "Felis"),
  Canis    = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Mammalia", "Carnivora", "Canidae", "Canis"),
  Homo     = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Mammalia", "Primates", "Hominidae", "Homo"),
  Musca    = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Arthropoda", "Insecta", "Diptera", "Muscidae", "Musca")
)
example <- taxo_from_lineages(
  lineages,
  ranks = setNames(rep(list(standard), length(lineages)), names(lineages))
)
d <- distance_matrix(example, metric = "ranked", progress = FALSE)

communities <- rbind(
  site_1 = c(Panthera = 4, Felis = 2, Canis = 1, Homo = 0, Musca = 0),
  site_2 = c(Panthera = 1, Felis = 0, Canis = 1, Homo = 2, Musca = 5)
)
taxo_distinctness(communities, d)

set.seed(1)
taxo_distinctness_test(c("Panthera", "Felis", "Canis"), d, n_iter = 499)

title: Introduction to taxodist
text:
Coverage, search, and homonyms
Use check_coverage() before a large calculation to identify names that cannot be resolved. Use taxo_search() to inspect possible Taxonomicon matches when a name is ambiguous or unexpected.

RPythonJulia


check_coverage(c("Tyrannosaurus", "Homo sapiens", "Fakeosaurus"))
taxo_search("Bacteria")
get_taxonomicon_id("Tyrannosaurus")


td.check_coverage(["Tyrannosaurus", "Homo sapiens", "Fakeosaurus"])
td.taxo_search("Bacteria")
td.get_taxonomicon_id("Tyrannosaurus")


check_coverage(["Tyrannosaurus", "Homo sapiens", "Fakeosaurus"])
taxo_search("Bacteria")
get_taxonomicon_id("Tyrannosaurus")



taxonomicon_available() checks quickly whether the server can be reached, which is useful before a long batch or in scripts and examples that should be skipped when there is no connection.
When a name has several biological entries, entries marked as invalid, rejected, nude, or illegitimate names (nom. inval., nom. rej., nom. nud., nom. illeg.) are considered only after the others.
When reproducibility matters, record the resolved numeric ID and the retrieval date. This helps distinguish homonyms and documents which external classification was queried.
check_coverage() distinguishes three outcomes: found, absent from The Taxonomicon, and unknown because the server could not be reached (NA in R, pd.NA in Python, missing in Julia). A temporary network failure is therefore not reported as missing coverage.

title: Introduction to taxodist
section: Resolve a complete input list before analysis
text:
Resolve a complete input list before analysis
taxo_resolve() provides an auditable resolution layer. Instead of discovering ambiguous or missing names while a distance matrix is being assembled, it records the decision for every input first.
Each row retains the original input, selected name and identifier, status, candidate count, lineage depth, lineage, and candidate table. Status is one of resolved, ambiguous, unresolved, or retrieval_error.

RPythonJulia


resolution <- taxo_resolve(
  c("Tyrannosaurus", "Nereis", "Unknown taxon", "50841"),
  ambiguity = "warn",
  progress = FALSE
)

resolution[, c("input", "resolved_name", "id", "status", "n_candidates")]
distance_matrix(resolution, progress = FALSE)


resolution = td.taxo_resolve(
    ["Tyrannosaurus", "Nereis", "Unknown taxon", "50841"],
    ambiguity="warn",
    progress=False,
)

resolution[["input", "resolved_name", "id", "status", "n_candidates"]]
td.distance_matrix(resolution, progress=False)


resolution = taxo_resolve(
    ["Tyrannosaurus", "Nereis", "Unknown taxon", "50841"];
    ambiguity="warn",
    progress=false,
)

resolution[:, [:input, :resolved_name, :id, :status, :n_candidates]]
distance_matrix(resolution; progress=false)



The ambiguity policy can warn and select the first valid candidate ("warn"), select it silently ("first"), or stop after auditing the inputs ("error"). Numeric Taxonomicon IDs bypass name search.
Homonyms in different parts of the classification can often be resolved automatically with within, which keeps only candidates whose lineage contains the given clade. Names without such a candidate are reported as unresolved.

RPythonJulia


taxo_resolve(c("Nereis", "Tyrannosaurus"), within = "Animalia")


td.taxo_resolve(["Nereis", "Tyrannosaurus"], within="Animalia")


taxo_resolve(["Nereis", "Tyrannosaurus"]; within="Animalia")



Each stored lineage is truncated at the queried taxon exactly as in get_lineage(), so a matrix computed from a resolution equals the matrix computed from the same names.






Why resolve first?



The resolution object separates absent names from retrieval failures, makes homonym choices inspectable, and reuses stored lineages in downstream matrix construction.

title: Introduction to taxodist
section: Work completely offline with curated lineages
text:
Work completely offline with curated lineages
taxo_from_lineages() creates the same auditable object without contacting an online service. This is useful for frozen classifications, unpublished taxonomies, manually reviewed lineages, and reproducible teaching examples.

RPythonJulia


local <- taxo_from_lineages(
  list(
    Alpha = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Alpha"),
    Beta = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Beta")
  ),
  source = "Curated study"
)

distance_matrix(local, progress = FALSE)


local = td.taxo_from_lineages(
    {
        "Alpha": ["Biota", "Animalia", "Alpha"],
        "Beta": ["Biota", "Animalia", "Beta"],
    },
    source="Curated study",
)

td.distance_matrix(local, progress=False)


local_lineages = taxo_from_lineages(
    [
        "Alpha" => ["Biota", "Animalia", "Alpha"],
        "Beta" => ["Biota", "Animalia", "Beta"],
    ];
    source="Curated study",
)

distance_matrix(local_lineages; progress=false)



In Julia, pass a vector of label => lineage pairs (or an ordered dictionary) to keep the input order; a plain Dict has no defined order, so its labels are sorted.
An optional ranks argument supplies the rank of every node (missing for unranked nodes). Ranks are needed only by the "ranked" metric; see the example under Taxonomic diversity and distinctness.

title: Introduction to taxodist
text:
Save a portable analysis bundle
A bundle preserves the resolution audit, matrix, metric definition, software metadata, and source provenance together. The JSON schema is shared by the R, Python, and Julia implementations.

RPythonJulia


bundle <- taxo_bundle(resolution, progress = FALSE)
write_taxodist_bundle(bundle, "analysis.taxodist.json")
restored <- read_taxodist_bundle("analysis.taxodist.json")
distance_matrix(restored)


bundle = td.taxo_bundle(resolution, progress=False)
td.write_taxodist_bundle(bundle, "analysis.taxodist.json")
restored = td.read_taxodist_bundle("analysis.taxodist.json")
td.distance_matrix(restored)


bundle = taxo_bundle(resolution; progress=false)
write_taxodist_bundle(bundle, "analysis.taxodist.json")
restored = read_taxodist_bundle("analysis.taxodist.json")
distance_matrix(restored)



Unlike cache files, bundle files are designed for cross-language exchange. Missing distances are stored as JSON null; disconnected positive or negative infinity uses the explicit strings "Infinity" and "-Infinity".
taxo_bundle() accepts metric. Bundles use schema 1.1, which records the metric (and, for "ranked", its rank levels) together with the lineage ranks, so the stored matrix can be verified from the stored lineages. Bundles written by earlier versions (schema 1.0) are still read.

Compare an analysis with a later repetition
Live classifications change. When an analysis is repeated, compare_bundles() reports which inputs changed status, identifier, or lineage, which were added or removed, and which pairwise distances changed as a consequence. Bundle files can be passed by path.

RPythonJulia


before <- read_taxodist_bundle("analysis.taxodist.json")
after <- taxo_bundle(before$resolution$input)
compare_bundles(before, after)


before = td.read_taxodist_bundle("analysis.taxodist.json")
after = td.taxo_bundle(list(before.resolution["input"]))
print(td.compare_bundles(before, after))


before = read_taxodist_bundle("analysis.taxodist.json")
after = taxo_bundle(before.resolution.input)
compare_bundles(before, after)

title: Introduction to taxodist
text:
Save and restore the cache
Retrieved identifiers and lineages are cached in memory. Saving the cache avoids repeating those network requests in a later session.

RPythonJulia


cache_info()
save_cache("taxodist-cache.rds")

clear_cache()
load_cache("taxodist-cache.rds")


td.cache_info()
td.save_cache("taxodist-cache.pkl")

td.clear_cache()
td.load_cache("taxodist-cache.pkl")


cache_info()
save_cache("taxodist-cache.json")

clear_cache()
load_cache("taxodist-cache.json")



The three implementations use language-specific cache formats: .rds in R, .pkl in Python, and .json in Julia. These cache files are not interchangeable. Python cache files use pickle; only load them from sources you trust.
Called without a file, save_cache() and load_cache() use a persistent per-user cache location: tools::R_user_dir("taxodist", "cache") in R and the platform’s user cache directory in Python and Julia (overridable with the TAXODIST_CACHE_DIR environment variable).
Lineages in cache files written before version 1.0.0 were produced by the earlier text parser; load_cache() discards them with a warning and keeps only the taxon identifiers, so they are retrieved again with the current parser.
Requests to The Taxonomicon are retried with exponential backoff after network errors and server errors. The number of attempts (default 3) is set with options(taxodist.max_tries = 5) in R, taxodist.fetch.MAX_TRIES = 5 in Python, and Taxodist.MAX_TRIES[] = 5 in Julia.
Consecutive requests are spaced by at least 0.25 seconds so that large batches do not overload the server. The interval is set with options(taxodist.min_interval = 0.5) in R, taxodist.fetch.MIN_INTERVAL = 0.5 in Python, and Taxodist.MIN_INTERVAL[] = 0.5 in Julia; 0 disables it.

The object records the date and package version with which it was generated (for version 1.0.0, rebuilt with the new lineage parser); it is a dated snapshot and may differ slightly from current live lineages. The native package objects remain language-specific.

title: taxodist
text:
Taxonomic hierarchy distances and lineage analysis in R, Python, and Julia
taxodist retrieves ordered taxonomic lineages and the ranks of their nodes, documents name-resolution decisions, and computes distances from the depth of the most recent common ancestor in the continuous shared lineage prefix. Path-length, Wu–Palmer, and rank-based distances and the taxonomic distinctness indices of Clarke and Warwick are also available.
Introduction and usage · Methodology · Function reference · Web application

title: taxodist
text:
What does taxodist measure?
For two ordered lineages \(L_A\) and \(L_B\), taxodist finds their continuous common prefix. Its final node is their most recent common ancestor (MRCA):
\[
d(A,B)=
\begin{cases}
0, & L_A = L_B, \\
\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA})}, & L_A \neq L_B.
\end{cases}
\]
A deeper shared ancestor produces a smaller distance. Zero is reserved for identical hierarchy nodes; distinct ancestor–descendant nodes retain a positive distance. This reciprocal distance is the default; the metric argument selects the path length, the Wu–Palmer distance, or a rank-based distance instead.






Classification distance, not evolutionary distance



These values describe separation within a recorded classification. They are not evolutionary time, genetic distance, morphological divergence, phylogenetic branch length, or evidence that a particular phylogeny is correct.


Detailed definition and assumptions

title: taxodist
text:
Version 1.0.0
Version 1.0.0 is the first stable release, published simultaneously for R, Python, and Julia. The default distance, the alternative metrics, and the bundle format (schema 1.1) are now stable: later 1.x releases keep their definitions and continue to read bundles written by this version.

New lineage parser. Lineages are read from the structure of The Taxonomicon page rather than from its text, so author strings, rank labels, and markers can no longer leak into, or remove, lineage nodes. Distances can differ from earlier versions.
Ranks. The rank of every lineage node is retrieved and cached with the lineage. lineage_ranks() returns each node with its rank and depth, and resolutions store the ranks.
Distance metrics. A metric argument selects "reciprocal" (default, unchanged), "path", "wu_palmer", or "ranked" (Clarke and Warwick’s step weights).
Taxonomic distinctness. taxo_distinctness() computes Δ, Δ*, Δ+, and Λ+ (agreeing with vegan::taxondive()), and taxo_distinctness_test() compares a sample with random draws from a species pool.
Bundle schema 1.1. Bundles record the metric and the lineage ranks; schema 1.0 bundles are still read.
Gentler on the server. Consecutive requests are spaced by at least 0.25 s, and taxonomicon_available() checks quickly whether the server can be reached.

See the changelog for the complete list, including breaking changes.

title: taxodist
text:
Data source and citation
Live lineages originate from The Taxonomicon, based on Systema Naturae 2000. Empirical work should record the package version, implementation, retrieval date, selected numeric identifiers, unresolved taxa, and lineage source.

Brands, S.J. (1989 onwards). Systema Naturae 2000. Amsterdam, The Netherlands. Retrieved from The Taxonomicon, http://taxonomicon.taxonomy.nl.

Introduction and usage · Cross-language compatibility

title: Methodology
text:
taxodist represents a taxon as an ordered sequence of hierarchy nodes retrieved from The Taxonomicon. The first element is the retained root and the final element is the queried node.
The distance is defined from the position of the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) in those ordered lineages. It is therefore a property of a taxonomic classification, not a direct measurement of evolutionary process.
Lineages are read from the structured hierarchy of each Taxonomicon page: every node is the scientific name marked up by the page itself, and the rank recorded for it is retained. Author strings, rank labels, and extinction or type markers are therefore not part of node names. Pages without the structured block are parsed from text by extracting the scientific name at the start of each line. This parser, introduced in version 1.0.0, is identical in the three implementations.
The reciprocal distance defined below is the default. Three alternatives are described under Alternative metrics.

title: Methodology
text:
Formal definition
Let \(L_A = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m)\) and \(L_B = (b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n)\) be the ordered lineages of nodes \(A\) and \(B\). Define the common-prefix depth as
\[
h(A,B) = \max\left\{k : a_i=b_i \text{ for every } i \leq k\right\}.
\]
When \(h(A,B)>0\), the node \(a_{h(A,B)}=b_{h(A,B)}\) is the MRCA under the source classification. The distance is
\[
d(A,B)=
\begin{cases}
0, & L_A=L_B, \\
\dfrac{1}{h(A,B)}, & L_A\neq L_B \text{ and } h(A,B)>0, \\
\infty, & h(A,B)=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Depth is counted from 1 at the retained root. Consequently, finite distances between distinct nodes lie in \((0,1]\).

Why the continuous prefix matters
Shared ancestry must be continuous from the root. A name that occurs in both lineages after their first disagreement is not treated as a shared ancestor. This prevents homonyms or repeated labels below different branches from producing an incorrect MRCA.
For example, consider
Biota → Animalia → Alpha → Homonym → A
Biota → Animalia → Beta  → Homonym → B
The MRCA is Animalia, not Homonym, because the lineages diverge before the repeated label.

title: Methodology
text:
Identity and ancestor–descendant pairs
Zero is reserved for identical complete lineages. Two different nodes always have positive finite distance when they belong to the same connected hierarchy.
Suppose \(A\) is an ancestor of \(B\). Then \(L_A\) is a proper prefix of \(L_B\), so the MRCA is \(A\) and
\[
d(A,B)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{depth}(A)}>0.
\]
This choice distinguishes node identity from containment:

use taxo_distance() to compare hierarchy nodes;
use is_member() to test whether a taxon belongs to a clade;
use taxo_path() to inspect the route connecting two nodes.

title: Methodology
text:
Ultrametric property
Within one connected hierarchy, the distance is non-negative, symmetric, and satisfies identity of indiscernibles. It also satisfies the strong triangle inequality
\[
d(A,C) \leq \max\{d(A,B),d(B,C)\}.
\]

Proof
If \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) belong to the same connected hierarchy, the common prefix of \(A\) and \(C\) must be at least as long as the shorter of the common prefixes of \((A,B)\) and \((B,C)\):
\[
h(A,C) \geq \min\{h(A,B),h(B,C)\}.
\]
For distinct nodes, taking positive reciprocals reverses the inequality:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{h(A,C)}
&\leq \frac{1}{\min\{h(A,B),h(B,C)\}} \\
&= \max\left\{\frac{1}{h(A,B)},\frac{1}{h(B,C)}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Cases involving identical nodes follow immediately because their distance is zero. Thus the strong triangle inequality holds.


Consequence
If two pairs of taxa share an MRCA at the same depth, both pairs receive the same distance. Differences in the number of recorded nodes below that MRCA do not affect their pairwise distance.
This produces tied distance levels corresponding to shared positions in the hierarchy. Such ties are an expected property of the measure, not numerical imprecision.

title: Methodology
section: Verification with the offline reference matrix
text:
Verification with the offline reference matrix
The ultrametric inequality can be checked using the fixed taxobase object.

RPythonJulia


library(taxodist)
data(taxobase, package = "taxodist")

m <- as.matrix(taxobase$statistical_matrix)
tol <- sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)

check_triplet <- function(index) {
  i <- index[1]
  j <- index[2]
  k <- index[3]

  d <- c(m[i, j], m[i, k], m[j, k])
  max(d) <= sort(d, decreasing = TRUE)[2] + tol
}

all(combn(seq_len(nrow(m)), 3, FUN = check_triplet))


from itertools import combinations
import numpy as np
import taxodist as td

taxobase = td.load_taxobase()
matrix = taxobase["statistical_matrix"]
if matrix.empty:
    matrix = taxobase["matrix"]
m = matrix.to_numpy()
tol = np.sqrt(np.finfo(float).eps)

def check_triplet(index):
    i, j, k = index
    distances = sorted(
        [m[i, j], m[i, k], m[j, k]],
        reverse=True,
    )
    return distances[0] <= distances[1] + tol

all(check_triplet(x) for x in combinations(range(len(m)), 3))


using Taxodist

taxobase = load_taxobase()
matrix = taxobase.statistical_matrix
m = Matrix(matrix)
tol = sqrt(eps(Float64))

function check_triplet(i, j, k)
    distances = sort([m[i, j], m[i, k], m[j, k]], rev=true)
    distances[1] <= distances[2] + tol
end

n = size(m, 1)
all(
    check_triplet(i, j, k)
    for i in 1:(n - 2) for j in (i + 1):(n - 1) for k in (j + 1):n
)



For an ultrametric triangle, the two largest pairwise distances are equal. The checks above allow a small numerical tolerance.

title: Methodology
text:
Alternative metrics
The reciprocal distance weights shallow divergences heavily: two taxa whose MRCA is at depth 2 are at distance 0.5, while MRCAs at depths 40 and 41 give 0.025 and 0.024. It is also sensitive to the uneven resolution of the classification: in The Taxonomicon, vertebrate lineages are typically several times deeper than bacterial ones, so equal values do not correspond to equivalent taxonomic levels in different groups.
The metric argument offers three alternatives. With \(h\) the MRCA depth and \(d_A\), \(d_B\) the depths of the two lineages:








Metric
Definition
Properties




"reciprocal" (default)
\(1/h\)
Ultrametric


"path"
\(d_A + d_B - 2h\)
Tree metric (number of edges); not an ultrametric when depths differ


"wu_palmer"
\(1 - 2h/(d_A + d_B)\)
In \([0,1)\); normalized by depth; not guaranteed to satisfy the triangle inequality


"ranked"
Half the path through the standard ranks only
Clarke and Warwick’s step weights



Every metric is zero for identical lineages. Lineages without a shared root have infinite distance, except under "wu_palmer", where their distance is 1. The ultrametric property and the tree representation described on this page apply to the reciprocal distance.
The "ranked" metric reduces each lineage to its root, the nodes of the Linnaean ranks kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species, and the queried taxon. Unranked clades, which make up most of the nodes of richly resolved groups, are ignored. For two species, the distance is the number of rank levels up to their shared rank: 1 in the same genus, 2 in the same family, and so on. The rank levels can be changed (taxodist.rank_levels in R, taxodist.distance.RANK_LEVELS in Python, Taxodist.RANK_LEVELS[] in Julia). The Taxonomicon follows current phylogenetic classifications, so that, for example, birds are the subclass Aves of the class Reptilia.

RPythonJulia


standard <- c(NA, "Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus")
lineages <- list(
  Panthera = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Mammalia", "Carnivora", "Felidae", "Panthera"),
  Felis    = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Mammalia", "Carnivora", "Felidae", "Felis"),
  Canis    = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Mammalia", "Carnivora", "Canidae", "Canis"),
  Homo     = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Chordata", "Mammalia", "Primates", "Hominidae", "Homo"),
  Musca    = c("Biota", "Animalia", "Arthropoda", "Insecta", "Diptera", "Muscidae", "Musca")
)
example <- taxo_from_lineages(
  lineages,
  ranks = setNames(rep(list(standard), length(lineages)), names(lineages))
)

for (metric in c("reciprocal", "path", "wu_palmer", "ranked")) {
  cat("\n", metric, "\n")
  print(round(distance_matrix(example, metric = metric, progress = FALSE), 3))
}

title: Methodology
text:
Taxonomic distinctness
taxo_distinctness() computes the indices of Warwick and Clarke: taxonomic diversity \(\Delta\), taxonomic distinctness \(\Delta^*\), average taxonomic distinctness \(\Delta^+\), and its variation \(\Lambda^+\). With the "ranked" metric they reproduce the classical definitions based on Linnaean ranks and agree with vegan::taxondive(); with the other metrics they use the full resolution of the classification.
\(\Delta^+\) and \(\Lambda^+\) use presence only and, unlike species richness, their expected values do not depend on sampling effort. taxo_distinctness_test() therefore compares a sample with random samples of the same number of taxa drawn from a master list. A \(\Delta^+\) below the lower limit indicates that the sample is less taxonomically distinct than expected from the pool. Worked examples are given in the guide and in Statistical Applications.

title: Methodology
Methodology
text:
Ambiguous, missing, and disconnected lineages

Ambiguous names
A scientific name may correspond to several biological entries. Entries marked as invalid, rejected, nude, or illegitimate names are considered only after the others, and taxo_resolve() can restrict candidates to a clade with within. Use taxo_search() to inspect candidates and supply a numeric Taxonomicon ID when a particular taxonomic concept is required.


Missing lineages
If a lineage cannot be retrieved, pairwise matrices retain the taxon label and use NA in R or NaN in Python and Julia for affected comparisons. Coverage should be examined before analysis.


Disconnected roots
Valid biological lineages retrieved and cleaned from The Taxonomicon retain Biota as their shared root. An infinite distance is therefore not expected during ordinary Taxonomicon use. It remains a defensive result for supplied or malformed lineages with no common initial node; this differs from a missing lineage because both inputs exist but are disconnected under the retained representation.
Clustering, ordination, and heatmap methods require a finite, complete matrix. The implementations check these conditions and return an informative fallback object when they are not satisfied.

title: Methodology
Methodology
text:
Tree representation of the classification
Because the distance is an ultrametric, the supplied taxa can be represented exactly by a rooted tree in which every pairwise distance equals the patristic distance between the corresponding tips. taxo_tree() constructs this tree directly from the lineages rather than by clustering.
Internal nodes correspond to clades at which the supplied taxa diverge; clades with a single descendant among the supplied taxa are omitted. A clade at depth \(h\) is placed at height \(1/(2h)\) and tips at height zero. For two taxa whose MRCA has depth \(h\), the path between them therefore has length
\[
\frac{1}{2h} + \frac{1}{2h} = \frac{1}{h} = d(A,B).
\]
A taxon that is an ancestor of another supplied taxon is attached to its clade node by a branch of length \(1/(2h)\), and taxa with identical lineages are joined at height zero, which preserves distances of \(1/h\) and \(0\) respectively.
Average-linkage clustering of an ultrametric matrix recovers the same hierarchy of distance levels, but stats::hclust() and comparable routines resolve tied levels into a sequence of binary merges. The tree built from the lineages instead keeps polytomies and labels each split with its clade name. Both are representations of the classification; neither is a phylogenetic estimate, and branch lengths are not evolutionary times.

title: Methodology
Methodology
text:
Recommended methods statement
A concise description may be adapted as follows:

Ordered taxonomic lineages were resolved from The Taxonomicon using taxodist version 1.0.0. Candidate matches, selected identifiers, resolution statuses, and retrieval dates were retained in an auditable resolution record. For distinct nodes, distance was defined as the reciprocal of the depth of their most recent common ancestor in the continuous common lineage prefix; identical complete lineages received distance zero. The resulting values represent classification depth rather than evolutionary time or phylogenetic branch length.

If another metric is used, replace the distance sentence with its definition, for example: “Distance was defined as half the number of steps between Linnaean rank levels (kingdom to species) separating the two taxa through their lowest shared rank (Clarke and Warwick, 1998).”
Report retrieval dates, unresolved taxa, and downstream analysis details separately.

taxodist 0.6.0

Distance definition

Zero distance is now reserved for identical complete lineages.
Distinct ancestor–descendant nodes receive \(1 / \operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA})\) rather than zero.
The measure is now described consistently as a taxonomic hierarchy distance, not a phylogenetic distance.
Within each connected hierarchy, the resulting distance is an ultrametric.







Behavioral change



Analyses that relied on version 0.5.0 or earlier should be recomputed when ancestor–descendant pairs are present. Use is_member() for clade containment and taxo_path() to inspect the route between hierarchy nodes.
